definition.text: Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959) was an English economist, best known for the idea of taxing activities that cause negative externalities.

facts.text: In The Economics of Welfare (1920) he introduced the externality concept and the idea that a tax could correct externality problems, now called a Pigouvian tax.
He argued that harmful side effects should be offset by a tax and beneficial ones by a subsidy.
He studied under Alfred Marshall and succeeded him as Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge in 1908.
In the early 1960s Ronald Coase criticised his analysis, arguing that taxes and subsidies are unnecessary if the parties can bargain.
The externality concept remains central to welfare economics and especially to environmental economics.
The Pigou Club, named after him, groups modern economists who back a carbon tax against climate change.

definition.text: Elinor Ostrom (1933–2012) was an American political scientist and political economist who showed how communities can manage shared resources themselves.

facts.text: Against the predictions of the tragedy of the commons, her field studies showed users of pastures, fisheries and forests making their own rules to manage them sustainably.
In Governing the Commons (1990) she summarized eight design principles shared by long-lasting common-pool resource institutions.
She favoured a polycentric approach, with key management decisions made as close as possible to the places and people involved, rather than a single global authority.
With co-researchers she built the Social-Ecological Systems (SES) framework for studying common-pool resources and self-governance.
In 2009 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Oliver E. Williamson.
The Nobel citation said her work showed common resources can be managed successfully without government regulation or privatization.
"Ostrom's law" sums up her challenge to theory: a resource arrangement that works in practice can work in theory.
